slides.title: Qafila's margin report is wrong, and nobody can say by how much
slides.text: The case for the week Qafila's margin report is wrong, and nobody can say by how much Qafila Trading : a fictional importer and wholesaler in Jeddah, Riyadh and Dammam 240 business customers, 18 suppliers in five countries, three currencies An order database, nightly extracts, a supplier price API, a change feed, shipment events All synthetic, written with a fixed seed: every number in this course can be reproduced Lujain Al-Zamil Finance controller. Signs the monthly margin. Does not trust it. Ammar Basri Procurement. Owns the supplier price feed. Dalia Sabri Margin analyst. Reads the mart; must not read customer contacts.

slides.title: The sales app and finance ask the same database opposite questions
slides.text: Transactional and analytical The sales app and finance ask the same database opposite questions Sales app (transactional) Finance (analytical) Rows touched a few, found by key millions, scanned Columns all of one row a few of every row Writes many small, concurrent none, or a nightly batch Who waits a person, in milliseconds a report, in seconds

slides.title: A row store keeps each order together; a column store keeps each field together
slides.text: Storage layout A row store keeps each order together; a column store keeps each field together Row store (SQLite, PostgreSQL) One read returns a whole order line. An index on order_id finds it without scanning. Summing one field reads every field. Column store (DuckDB, warehouses) A sum reads only qty, unit_price_sar and discount_pct, compressed and in batches. Fetching one whole row touches every column file.

slides.title: Each engine wins its own question by more than ten times
slides.text: Lab 1.1 · full run, 552,090 lines Each engine wins its own question by more than ten times Point lookup (one order) Monthly aggregate SQLite (rows, indexed) 0.04 ms 662 ms DuckDB (columns) 1.87 ms 56 ms Same lines, same SQL, one laptop. Your numbers will differ; the direction will not.

slides.title: Copy first, transform where the analysis runs
slides.text: ELT Copy first, transform where the analysis runs Extract nightly copy of orders → Load unchanged, into raw → Transform SQL in the analytical engine Loading before transforming keeps the evidence: a wrong rule can be fixed and re-run on the raw copy. The transformation runs on the engine built for scans, not on the order database.

slides.title: Raw, staging and marts: each layer has one job
slides.text: Layered refinement Raw, staging and marts: each layer has one job Raw Exactly as received, dated, never edited. The extracts, the API pages, the change feed. Staging Typed, deduplicated, one row per key. One model per source table. Marts Facts and dimensions that answer finance's questions. Tested. Some teams call them bronze, silver and gold. The names matter less than the rule: each layer reads only the one before.

slides.title: Warehouse, lake, lakehouse: where the tables live and who can read them
slides.text: Three platform shapes Warehouse, lake, lakehouse: where the tables live and who can read them Shape Storage Read by Good at Warehouse the engine's own format that engine modelled, tested tables; SQL Lake open files (Parquet, JSON) on object storage any engine cheap raw history; no tables, no transactions Lakehouse open files plus an open table format several engines tables with snapshots and schema changes over open files

slides.title: DuckDB runs inside Python and reads files where they are
slides.text: An analytical engine in your notebook DuckDB runs inside Python and reads files where they are import duckdb con = duckdb.connect() con.sql(""" SELECT status, count(*) AS orders FROM read_csv('data/raw/extracts/orders.csv') GROUP BY ALL""") No server, no load step: a CSV, Parquet or JSON file is a table. The same SQL later runs on a warehouse.

slides.title: Profile the grain before you add anything up
slides.text: Before any sum Profile the grain before you add anything up 18,630 lines in the extract 18,403 distinct (order, line) keys Two questions first: what is one row (the grain), and do the keys say so? Here they do not: 227 lines are there twice.

slides.title: A join can multiply rows as easily as it drops them
slides.text: Joins A join can multiply rows as easily as it drops them Join What happens to the order lines lines to orders on order_id same count: each line has one order lines to prices on product_id only one row per price version: the count grows orders to customers, inner orders of an erased customer disappear Count before and after every join. A join that changes the count without a reason you can state is a defect.

slides.title: Join each line to the price valid on its order date
slides.text: Cost at the right price Join each line to the price valid on its order date JOIN read_csv('prices.csv') AS pr ON pr.product_id = l.product_id AND o.order_date BETWEEN pr.valid_from AND coalesce(pr.valid_to, DATE '9999-12-31') 58 products, 102 price versions: prices changed inside the quarter. Costing with today's price moves last month's margin every time procurement updates a price. Cartons become pieces first: qty * units_per_carton.

slides.title: Window functions
slides.text: Session 3 Window functions Write a running total with a window frame Detect changes with LAG over an ordered partition Keep one row per group with ROW_NUMBER and QUALIFY 03

slides.title: GROUP BY collapses rows; a window keeps them and adds a value
slides.text: GROUP BY and OVER GROUP BY collapses rows; a window keeps them and adds a value SELECT order_date, sum(revenue) FROM mart.fct_order_line GROUP BY order_date SELECT order_id, revenue, sum(revenue) OVER ( PARTITION BY order_date) FROM mart.fct_order_line One September week: 7 rows on the left, 1,228 on the right, each with its day's total beside it.

slides.title: Partition says where it restarts, order says what "so far" means
slides.text: Three parts of OVER Partition says where it restarts, order says what "so far" means sum(margin) OVER ( PARTITION BY month -- restart each month ORDER BY order_date -- "so far" in date order ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) -- the frame The last day of each month equals finance's monthly margin: 5,413,128 riyals for August.

slides.title: LAG compares each price with the one before it
slides.text: The previous row LAG compares each price with the one before it lag(cost_piece_sar) OVER ( PARTITION BY product_id ORDER BY valid_from) AS previous_cost Product From Previous New Change P-1004 13 Sep 2.73 3.06 +12.1% P-1019 15 Aug 14.51 16.24 +11.9% P-1016 22 Aug 28.08 31.27 +11.4%

slides.title: ROW_NUMBER and QUALIFY keep the first or last row of each group
slides.text: One row per group ROW_NUMBER and QUALIFY keep the first or last row of each group SELECT * FROM stg.orders QUALIFY row_number() OVER ( PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY created_at DESC) = 1 The same pattern deduplicates the re-sent lines of Lab 1.2 and picks the latest change event on Day 2. Windows run after WHERE, so WHERE cannot filter them; QUALIFY can.

slides.title: Recompute only the month that changed
slides.text: Incremental predicates Recompute only the month that changed 17,665 lines read by a full recompute 6,075 lines read for October alone A predicate on the partition you know changed (order_date >= DATE '2026-10-01') turns a rebuild into an update. The result must equal the full recompute: test that.

slides.text: Checkpoint A running total that never resets Your margin-to-date keeps growing across August, September and October instead of restarting on the first of each month. What is missing? PARTITION BY month in the window ORDER BY month instead of order_date A GROUP BY month around the query ROWS BETWEEN 30 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW

slides.title: Columnar files and partitioning
slides.text: Session 4 Columnar files and partitioning Convert row files to Parquet and compare size and scan time Read row-group statistics and see which groups a filter skips Partition by month and measure what a one-month query reads 04

slides.title: The same lines as Parquet are seven times smaller and scan 25 times faster
slides.text: Lab 1.4 · full run, 745,200 lines The same lines as Parquet are seven times smaller and scan 25 times faster CSV size 71.1 MB Parquet size 9.6 MB CSV scan 545 ms Parquet scan 21 ms

slides.title: Each row group keeps the minimum and maximum of every column
slides.text: Inside a Parquet file Each row group keeps the minimum and maximum of every column A reader checks the footer first and skips the row groups whose range cannot match the filter. Shuffled rows: every group spans every date, so nothing is skipped. Sorted rows: each group covers a few days. Rows Groups that may hold 14 Sep shuffled 7 of 7 sorted by date 2 of 15

slides.title: A folder per month lets the reader skip whole files
slides.text: Partitioning A folder per month lets the reader skip whole files COPY big TO 'by_month' (FORMAT parquet, PARTITION_BY (month)); -- by_month/month=2026-08/… month=2026-09/… month=2026-10/… SELECT … FROM read_parquet('by_month/*/*.parquet', hive_partitioning = true) WHERE month = '2026-09' -- Scanning Files: 1/3 The September query reads 2.8 MB of 9.6 MB. At this size the time hardly changes; on object storage the bytes are the bill.

slides.title: Partition by day and customer and a full scan is 180 times slower
slides.text: The opposite mistake Partition by day and customer and a full scan is 180 times slower 3,841 files, most under a kilobyte 15 ms → 2,725 ms one file against all of them Every file has a footer to open and a request to make. Partition on a column that queries filter by and that has few values.

slides.title: The query that reads everything
slides.text: Checkpoint The query that reads everything The lines are partitioned by month, yet a query for September still scans all three folders. The filter is WHERE strftime(order_date, '%Y-%m') = '2026-09'. Why? Parquet cannot prune folders The row groups are not sorted Three folders are too few to prune The filter is on order_date, not on the partition column month

slides.title: Ingesting from APIs
slides.text: Session 1 Ingesting from APIs Follow every page of a cursor-paginated API Back off on 429 responses Store load state with the data so a re-run adds nothing 01

slides.title: Twenty records a page, a cursor to the next, and a 429 every few calls
slides.text: Qafila's supplier price API Twenty records a page, a cursor to the next, and a 429 every few calls {"data": [{"price_id": "PR-00009", "product_id": "P-1006", "supplier_name": "مؤسسة حبوب الحجاز", "cost": "81.22", "currency": "SAR", "unit": "carton", "valid_from": "2026-07-01", "updated_at": "2026-06-24T20:17:00+03:00"}, …], "next_cursor": "WyIiLCAyMF0="} Corrections come back later with the same price_id and a newer updated_at. The cursor is opaque: send it back, never parse it.

slides.title: Follow every page; on a 429, wait and repeat the same request
slides.text: Lab 2.1 · step 2 Follow every page; on a 429, wait and repeat the same request while True: resp = requests.get(f"{base}/prices", params=params, timeout=10) if resp.status_code == 429: time.sleep(float(resp.headers.get("Retry-After", "1"))) continue # same params: same page resp.raise_for_status() page = resp.json(); records += page["data"] if not page["next_cursor"]: break params = {"cursor": page["next_cursor"]}

slides.title: A key and a stored cursor make a load safe to repeat
slides.text: Loads that can run twice A key and a stored cursor make a load safe to repeat A key for one record version (price_id, updated_at), enforced on insert. A version loaded twice is stored once. The cursor stored with the data The highest updated_at loaded, in a table of the same database. The next run asks only for what is newer. Idempotent means running it again changes nothing. Retries, restarts and backfills all depend on it.

slides.title: The second run adds nothing; new data adds exactly the new versions
slides.text: Lab 2.1 · step 4 The second run adds nothing; new data adds exactly the new versions Run Rows inserted Requests First, API as of 15 October 99 7 Again, nothing new 0 1 After 31 October 28: 3 new prices, 25 corrections 2 Raw keeps both versions of each corrected price: 102 prices, 127 versions.

slides.title: Store the rows and the cursor in one transaction
slides.text: The failure in between Store the rows and the cursor in one transaction BEGIN → Insert new versions → Update the cursor → COMMIT Cursor first and a crash loses data silently. Rows first and a crash re-reads, which the key absorbs. Both together and neither can happen.

slides.title: The doubled table
slides.text: Checkpoint The doubled table A colleague's supplier load stores the cursor correctly, but after a crash and a re-run the table holds twice the rows for one day. Which decision was missing? A smaller page size Keeping the cursor in a file More retries on 429 A key on the record version, enforced on insert

slides.title: Declare the key, the cursor and the merge; the library does the rest
slides.text: Declarative ingestion Declare the key, the cursor and the merge; the library does the rest @dlt.resource(name="supplier_prices", primary_key="price_id", write_disposition="merge") def supplier_prices(base_url, updated_at=dlt.sources.incremental("updated_at", initial_value="")): params = {"updated_since": updated_at.last_value} … # the same paging loop as Lab 2.1 yield page["data"] pipeline.run(supplier_prices(api.url))

slides.title: Evolve in raw; decide on purpose everywhere after it
slides.text: What should a pipeline do with a new column? Evolve in raw; decide on purpose everywhere after it evolve Add the column. Nothing is lost. The default. freeze Fail the load. Someone decides. discard value Load the row, drop the field. discard row Skip the whole record. The stretch of Lab 2.2 freezes the columns: a record with an unknown field fails the load and the table is unchanged.

slides.title: Change data capture, merge and history
slides.text: Session 3 Change data capture, merge and history Read a change event envelope and order events by log position Apply updates and deletes to a copy with MERGE Keep history as a type 2 dimension with valid ranges 03

slides.title: Read the database's log, not its tables
slides.text: Change data capture Read the database's log, not its tables Supplier table procurement edits → Write-ahead log every committed change → Change events c, u, d with before and after → Your copy merged, and history Polling the table with "changed since" misses deletes and every change between two polls. The log has all of them, in commit order.

slides.title: The envelope carries the row before, the row after and the log position
slides.text: One change event The envelope carries the row before, the row after and the log position {"op": "u", "before": {"supplier_id": "S-07", "country": "AE", "currency": "AED", …}, "after": {"supplier_id": "S-07", "country": "SA", "currency": "SAR", …}, "source": {"table": "suppliers", "lsn": 7006317, "ts_ms": 1788242880000}, "ts_ms": 1788242880298} source.lsn: the order the database committed. ts_ms outside: when the event was sent. A delete has after null; a create has before null.

slides.title: Delivery repeats and reorders; the log position does not
slides.text: Lab 2.3 · step 1 Delivery repeats and reorders; the log position does not Arrival lsn Change to supplier S-15 11 7,005,180 e-mail becomes accounts6@… 12 7,004,499 payment terms 30 days (older) 13 7,005,956 e-mail becomes accounts7@… 38 events: 3 delivered twice, 1 after a newer change. Applied by arrival, event 12 would put the old e-mail back.

slides.title: MERGE applies the latest change per supplier in one statement
slides.text: Lab 2.3 · step 2 MERGE applies the latest change per supplier in one statement MERGE INTO suppliers AS t USING latest AS s ON t.supplier_id = s.sid WHEN MATCHED AND s.op = 'd' THEN DELETE WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET name_en = s.name_en, country = s.country, … WHEN NOT MATCHED AND s.op <> 'd' THEN INSERT (…) VALUES (…) 18 suppliers, S-12 deleted, S-19 and S-20 created: 19 rows, and EXCEPT both ways against the source finds nothing.

slides.title: A type 2 dimension keeps one row per version, with a validity range
slides.text: History A type 2 dimension keeps one row per version, with a validity range supplier country valid_from valid_to S-07 AE 1 Aug 1 Sep S-07 SA 1 Sep (current) S-12 TR 1 Aug 10 Oct (deleted) 52 versions, 19 current, no overlapping ranges. valid_from inclusive, valid_to exclusive: every moment belongs to one version.

slides.title: Two events, which one wins?
slides.text: Checkpoint Two events, which one wins? Two updates for supplier S-15 reach your pipeline. The second to arrive has a lower log position than the first. Which one should your copy keep? The one that arrived last The one with the later outer ts_ms The one with the higher log position Either: they will reconcile later

slides.title: A Polars expression is a rule you can name, run and log
slides.text: Cleaning with dataframes A Polars expression is a rule you can name, run and log RULES = [ ("digits", "cost_text", pl.col("cost").str.strip_chars() .str.replace_many(list("٠١٢٣٤٥٦٧٨٩٫"), list("0123456789.")) .str.replace(",", ".", literal=True)), ("to_sar", "cost_sar", pl.col("cost_text").cast(pl.Float64) * pl.col("currency").replace_strict(RATES, return_dtype=pl.Float64)), ]

slides.title: 102 prices, three currencies, two units, 56 spellings of 18 suppliers
slides.text: Lab 2.4 · step 1 102 prices, three currencies, two units, 56 spellings of 18 suppliers Cost as sent Means 81.22 81.22 ٣٫٣٣ 3.33, Arabic-Indic digits 36,09 36.09, decimal comma 21 costs are not plain decimals. USD at 3.75 and AED at 1.0211 riyals: the course's fixed rates. Most prices are per carton; cost per piece needs the product's units per carton.

slides.title: Five rules turn 56 spellings into 18 supplier ids
slides.text: Lab 2.4 · step 4 Five rules turn 56 spellings into 18 supplier ids Rule Example Trim spaces " أرز كيرلا " to "أرز كيرلا" Drop a company prefix "شركة", "مؤسسة" Remove tatweel "كيرلـا" to "كيرلا" One alef أ إ آ to ا One final taa ة to ه Normalise both sides the same way, then join. Every record must map, and to its product's supplier.

slides.title: Where rounding goes
slides.text: Checkpoint Where rounding goes A price is 61.99 USD per carton of 6. Your colleague converts to riyals, rounds to two decimals, then divides by 6 and rounds again. The ERP shows a different halala. What do you change? Divide by 6 before converting the currency Round once, after both steps Round the ERP's value the same way Store the cost as a 64-bit float

slides.title: Expand, migrate, then contract: both fields live until the last consumer moves
slides.text: A rename that breaks no one Expand, migrate, then contract: both fields live until the last consumer moves 1.0.0 freight_sar only → 1.1.0 expand add freight_cost; fill both; a rule says they agree → Migrate consumers move one at a time; freight_sar still filled → 2.0.0 contract drop freight_sar Adding a field breaks nobody, so it is a minor version. Removing one breaks whoever still reads it, so it waits, and it is a major version.

slides.title: A deleted row stays in its file until maintenance removes it
slides.text: Deletes and maintenance A deleted row stays in its file until maintenance removes it Operation What it writes What it leaves behind Delete or update a row a rewritten data file, or a deletion vector marking the row's position the old file, still read by earlier snapshots Many small appends many small data files slow scans: Day 1's small-files problem Compaction fewer, larger files with the deletes applied the replaced files, until they expire Expire snapshots shorter history nothing: files no snapshot needs are deleted Maintenance is scheduled like any other asset. Until it runs, "deleted" means "hidden from the current snapshot".

slides.title: Partitions, shuffles and stages
slides.text: Distributed processing Partitions, shuffles and stages Partitions The data split into pieces that workers process in parallel. Shuffle Rows move between workers so equal keys meet: for joins and group-bys. The expensive step. Stages The work between two shuffles; a stage ends where data must move.

slides.title: A small table is broadcast, so the join needs no shuffle
slides.text: Lab 4.2 · step 3 A small table is broadcast, so the join needs no shuffle Sum(TreeReduce) Sum(GroupByChunk) Filter: valid_from <= order_date <= valid_to BlockwiseMerge: on product_id FromPandas npartitions=8 (the lines) FromPandas npartitions=1 (102 prices) Each partition of lines meets the whole price list where it is; the month sums combine in a tree.

slides.title: At a million lines, one node is 160 times faster and uses a 27th of the memory
slides.text: Lab 4.2 · full run At a million lines, one node is 160 times faster and uses a 27th of the memory Lines DuckDB, one node Dask, local cluster 176,650 0.13 s 5.8 s 1,059,900 0.16 s, 9 MB 26.7 s, 243 MB 4,239,600 0.51 s 95.8 s The cluster never caught up on a 32 GB laptop. Same answer from both, to the riyal.

slides.title: Choose a cluster when one machine cannot hold the work, not before
slides.text: The decision Choose a cluster when one machine cannot hold the work, not before The data, with the working space of the query, no longer fits one machine's memory and disk. A deadline that one machine cannot meet, shown by a measurement. Many independent jobs at once, where the cluster is shared. Qafila: three months of lines are a few megabytes. Ten years would be under a gigabyte. One node.

slides.title: A log, offsets and consumer groups
slides.text: Streaming fundamentals A log, offsets and consumer groups Producers append events; each gets the next offset. A consumer group commits the offset it will read next, so a restart resumes there. Several groups read the same log independently: operations and finance each have their own position. Lab 4.3 2,312 shipment events, one partition, read in batches of 100, committed after each batch.

slides.title: A crash before the commit replays the batch: count by key, not by event
slides.text: Lab 4.3 · step 2 A crash before the commit replays the batch: count by key, not by event 747 deliveries, counting events 709 deliveries, by shipment id The consumer crashed at offset 1,049 with its last commit at 1,000, and the carriers sent 55 events twice. Keyed by shipment, the replay changes nothing.

slides.title: Window by when it happened; close the window when the watermark passes
slides.text: Event time Window by when it happened; close the window when the watermark passes Event time delivered on 21 October → Watermark latest event time minus allowed lateness → Window closes 21 October emitted → Late event dropped and logged

slides.title: A longer watermark answers later and drops less
slides.text: Lab 4.3 · step 4 and stretch A longer watermark answers later and drops less 1 hour 22 dropped 1 day 9 dropped 3 days 0 dropped Every delivery the stream misses is a late event the watermark dropped; the daily batch recount (709 deliveries) repairs it.

Short, with the late events logged and the batch reconciling Three days, so nothing is ever dropped No watermark: count events as they arrive Replace the stream with the nightly batch

slides.title: Qafila's margin mart, from the raw extracts to an Iceberg table
slides.text: What you build Qafila's margin mart, from the raw extracts to an Iceberg table Ingest the API and the change feed; supplier history as type 2. Model a star at order-line grain, cost as of the order date. Test and reconcile with finance's five answers. Gate each batch with the contract: a broken one changes nothing. Store the mart as Iceberg, read by a second engine. Govern the fields: register, masking, access tests. Starter: labs/capstone/pipeline.py has the nine steps, each naming the lab it reuses. The first is done.

slides.title: The assessor clones your repository and runs it from nothing
slides.text: Reproducibility The assessor clones your repository and runs it from nothing git clone <your repository> # then the commands of your README; with the starter: cd <it>/labs && uv sync uv run python capstone/pipeline.py uv run python capstone/pipeline.py --batch broken uv run python capstone/pipeline.py --backfill 2026-10 Run Must show Fixed batch row counts and test results equal to your README Broken batch the contract's failed checks, and the mart not refreshed Second run no new rows from the API Backfill one month rebuilt, the others untouched Clone it yourself first, into a new folder. A file only on your laptop fails the run.

slides.title: The rubric
slides.text: How the repository is scored The rubric Correctness of the mart 25% Ingestion and history 20% Tests and contract 20% Orchestration and recovery 15% Table format and governance 10% Reproducibility 10% The repository is 60% of your result and needs at least 60% on this rubric. The defence is 20%, the supervised checks 20%. The pass mark is 70% overall.

slides.title: Eight minutes for each defence
slides.text: Format Eight minutes for each defence 3 · One modelling decision What you chose, the alternative, and the number that shows you were right. 3 · A transformation we pick What it reads, what it writes, and what would break it. 2 · The broken batch The run log: what was caught, what stayed in place. AI-full. Coding agents were allowed. Explaining what they wrote is part of the defence.
